content.text: A merge and a rebase can leave you with exactly the same files; what differs is the history. A merge keeps every existing commit and adds one that joins two lines of work. A rebase copies your commits onto a new base as new commits with new IDs. That's fine for commits only you have, and it breaks things for anyone who built on the originals.
Sara and Omar share a branch called
. Before review, Sara wants a tidy history, so she rebases the branch onto
. Git rejects her push, so she adds

. The next morning Omar pulls, and his log shows "Add coupon field" twice, "Validate coupon codes" twice, and a merge commit he never meant to make. No code is missing, yet the branch now tells the same story twice, and every reviewer asks which copy is the real one.
The belief: rebase is just a cleaner merge. It produces the same code with a straighter history, so you can use it on any branch, shared ones included. If the push is rejected afterwards,

The belief has good support. Pro Git itself says of the two: "There is no difference in the end product of the integration, but rebasing makes for a cleaner history." A linear log is easier to scan, which is why some teams ask for one before review. As far as the files go, the belief is exactly right.
What it misses is that a rebase doesn't move your commits. It replaces them.
A merge adds one commit and changes nothing else
docs describe it: Git takes the other branch's changes since the two diverged and records the result "in a new commit along with the names of the two parent commits." That
is the only new object. Every existing commit keeps its ID, so anyone who already has them is unaffected.

Pro Git explains the mechanics: rebase works by "getting the diff introduced by each commit of the branch you're on, saving those diffs to temporary files, resetting the current branch to the same commit as the branch you are rebasing onto, and finally applying each change in turn." Each replayed change becomes a new

with a new parent, and because a commit's ID is a hash of its content, parent included, it gets a new ID. In the book's words: "When you rebase stuff, you're abandoning existing commits and creating new ones that are similar but different."
Here's Sara's branch integrated both ways, on Git 2.54:

blocks.code:
git log --oneline main..coupons
# e8ea870 Validate coupon codes
# 8289bcb Add coupon field
git switch -q -c try-merge coupons && git merge -q --no-edit main
git switch -q -c try-rebase coupons && git rebase -q main
git log --no-walk --format='%h %t %s' try-merge try-rebase
# 834ad14 0bf12b3 Validate coupon codes
# c923a93 0bf12b3 Merge branch 'main' into try-merge

content.text: , is the tree: the snapshot of every file. It's
for both, so the code is identical. The first column isn't: "Validate coupon codes" was
. Pro Git puts it exactly: "it's only the history that is different."
Shared commits make the difference matter

New IDs are harmless while nobody else has the old ones. Once a teammate has pulled them and built on them, their clone still holds the originals, and Git sees the rewritten copies as different commits. The

docs are blunt: "Rebasing (or any other form of rewriting) a branch that others have based work on is a bad idea: anyone downstream of it is forced to manually fix their history." Pro Git reduces it to one rule: "Do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on."
The fix: merge what's shared, rebase what's yours
Both sessions are Omar's clone, after Sara updated the shared branch in two different ways:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
# Sara ran: git rebase main, then git push --force
git pull --no-rebase   # Omar, with one unpushed commit
# From ../shop
#  + b3086e8...d707e50 coupons    -> origin/coupons  (forced update)
# Merge made by the 'ort' strategy.
git log --oneline --graph
# *   f7d87bc Merge branch 'coupons' of ../shop into coupons
# |\
# | * d707e50 Validate coupon codes
# | * 9356d40 Add coupon field
# | * 4680f97 Add shipping to total
# * | 14e1e70 Show coupon errors
# * | b3086e8 Validate coupon codes
# * | 2abf6f9 Add coupon field
# |/
# * 86434d1 Add checkout

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
# Sara ran: git merge --no-edit main, then git push
git pull --rebase   # Omar replays only his unpushed commit
# From ../shop
#    423afde..e9367a2  coupons    -> origin/coupons
# Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/coupons.
git log --oneline --graph
# * 0435bf2 Show coupon errors
# *   e9367a2 Merge branch 'main' into coupons
# |\
# | * 65f5f84 Add shipping to total
# * | 423afde Validate coupon codes
# * | 42d4aa8 Add coupon field
# |/
# * fc07af2 Add checkout
git push
# To ../shop.git
#    e9367a2..0435bf2  coupons -> coupons

items.text: Merge and rebase can produce the same files; only the history differs.
A merge adds one commit with two parents and leaves every existing commit untouched.
A rebase replaces your commits with new copies that have new IDs.
Never rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on.
